summary:
AstroHealth — 2026 NASA Space Apps ChallengeAstroHealth tackles the challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions" through a dual-level solution: a custom, bare-metal operating system and a concept hardware platform, ASTRO-BOOK.   1. AstroHealth OS (Software)
Built from scratch in freestanding C and x86 assembly (~3,800 lines across 23 files), AstroHealth OS eliminates external dependencies to ensure maximum reliability on flight hardware. Booting via GRUB Multiboot2 into 32-bit protected mode (1024×768×32 framebuffer), the kernel integrates custom interrupt handling, PS/2 keyboard support, a 8×16 bitmap font, and a custom UI kit. Its core telemetry engine (telemetry.c) processes physiological readings into color-coded green, yellow, and red status indicators for instant crew assessment. The build compiles into a bootable ISO (astrohealth.iso) verifiable in QEMU, backed by a 9-milestone roadmap mapping OS features directly to mission requirements.   2. ASTRO-BOOK (Concept Hardware)
Complementing the OS is ASTRO-BOOK, a solar-powered medical laptop concept powered by an 8-core RISC-V SoC (32 TOPS NPU) and a radiation-hardened 2TB NVMe SSD storing an offline medical atlas. Equipped with non-invasive, zero-radiation sensors—including QUS bone ultrasound, ECG palm pads, and BIA—alongside lockstep safety cores and SEL protection, the system enables autonomous, real-time crew diagnostics without relying on delayed Earth communications.
details:
Project Details — AstroHealth OS + ASTRO-BOOK
What exactly does it do?
AstroHealth OS is an operating system built from scratch whose native, built-in application is an autonomous astronaut crew health monitor (for the 2026 Space Apps challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions"). When it boots, it presents a full mission console that tracks, for a crew of 4:

Vitals per crew member: heart rate, SpO₂, core temperature, blood pressure, respiration rate, HRV, and a Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) reaction-time test for fatigue.
Environment: radiation dose rate + lifetime dose, CO₂ / CO₂ partial pressure, cabin pressure, and ICP/ONSD estimates (intracranial pressure — the Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome risk).
At-a-glance color coding: every indicator is classified OK / CAUTION / WARN with green–yellow–red status, an alert feed with acknowledgements, trend history charts (160 samples per metric), a live animated ECG/PPG waveform, a clickable human body map where each body system shows its metric, finding, and recommended action, and an anomaly/scenario engine (you can inject a medical event and watch the system detect, alert, and guide).
Clinical decision support: when a reading goes red, the system displays concrete guidance on what to do — not just the number.
Alongside the OS, we designed ASTRO-BOOK — the concept hardware it would run on: a 2.77 kg solar-powered space medical laptop integrating an octa-core radiation-hardened RISC-V SoC with a 32-TOPS NPU, a 2 TB rad-hard NVMe SSD, medical sensors (6-lead ECG + BIA palm pads, QUS bone-density probe with zero radiation, CMUT ultrasound, LOC blood-analysis lab, 60 GHz contactless radar), a cold-plasma sterilization waste unit, and an integrated triple-junction solar array — documented with a full electrical schematic and an interactive 3D model.

How does it work?
The OS is real, working software, not a mockup. It is a freestanding 32-bit C kernel with no libc: GRUB boots it via a Multiboot2 header, the kernel parses the Multiboot2 framebuffer tag to get a 1024×768×32 display, sets up its own IDT/interrupt system, runs a PIT-driven 100 Hz scheduler loop (~25 fps render loop), and drives polled PS/2 keyboard + mouse input. On top of that we wrote our own mini GUI framework (windows, buttons, widgets, 8×16 bitmap font, rounded rects, gradients) and the telemetry/clinical engine in pure C.
Build pipeline: NASM (boot/ISR asm) + i686 GCC (freestanding C) → ld with a custom linker script → grub-mkrescue → bootable ISO (tested in QEMU; the repo ships astrohealth.iso and astrohealth.bin).
The concept hardware is specified with a complete electrical architecture: a 28 V mil-spec power tree through a GaN multi-stage PMIC (96.8% efficiency) feeding regulated rails (+12 V pumps, +5 V sonar/touch, +3.3 V SSD, 0.8–1.0 V CPU core), a 4 kV galvanic isolation barrier for the medical analog front-end, and a system bus matrix (MIPI-DSI, LVDS/SPI, I²C/UART, SpaceWire/MIL-STD-1553, PWM actuator lines) — all drawn in the schematic SVG, with the physical layout as a Wavefront OBJ model and a Three.js viewer with exploded view, part inspection, and lid/explode animation.
What benefits does it have?
Zero ground dependence: all diagnosis, alerting, and guidance run locally on the spacecraft — no downlink latency, no connectivity required.
One glance, whole crew: color-coded status bands mean a crewmember without medical training can spot a problem in seconds; the body map turns an abnormal number into "what it affects → what to do."
Radiation-free diagnostics where it matters: bone density via ultrasound (QUS) instead of X-ray DEXA; contactless radar and optical/impedance sensors instead of invasive hardware; cold-plasma sterilization instead of consumable biocides.
Built to survive space: the hardware spec addresses the actual failure modes of computing in space — latch-up immunity, TMR registers, pSLC flash with STT-MRAM cache for 20-year data retention, AES-256 hardware encryption for private medical records.
Lightweight and verifiable: the OS boots in seconds on any x86 machine from a single 55 KB kernel — no cloud, no container, no dependencies.
What do you hope to achieve?
Complete the OS roadmap: chart engine polish, a timed-measurement scheduler (mission routine reminders), gamification (points/streaks to keep crews engaged with daily health tasks), and environment profiles (ship / station / rover / lunar base).
Demonstrate that a purpose-built OS — where the health app is the kernel's first-class citizen, not an afterthought app on Linux — is a credible architecture for autonomous crew health autonomy on Artemis-era missions.
Have the interactive 3D hardware concept serve as a concrete, reviewable vision of the flight computer this software targets.
Tools, languages, and software used
Languages: C (freestanding, GNU C11, no libc) and x86 assembly (NASM) for the OS; HTML/CSS/JavaScript (Three.js r128, canvas-generated textures) for the interactive 3D viewer; Mermaid for architecture diagrams; Wavefront OBJ for the hardware model.
Toolchain: GCC (-m32 -ffreestanding -fno-pie -mno-sse), NASM, GNU ld with custom linker.ld, grub-file/grub-mkrescue/xorriso, GNU Make.
Testing/debugging: QEMU (qemu-system-i386, with GTK display and GDB remote-debug target), serial-port logging, VGA text fallback for early boot errors.
Design/diagramming: hand-built SVG electrical schematic (power tree, compute/storage core, isolated medical AFE, dual-touch display controller), Mermaid flowcharts (boot flow, build pipeline, dashboard layout).
Platform: Ubuntu Linux development machine; everything builds with make and runs with make run.
